title: Oracy In Practice
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington responds to critics who set oracy against knowledge and standards, calling this a false binary. For him learning through talk has run through his thinking about great teaching for fourteen years, from probing questioning to Martin Robinson's Trivium 21c, and he sees a large gap in everyday practice where students are rarely given time to grapple with half-formed ideas. He then walks through the five Voice 21 benchmarks and shows how each layers onto a knowledge-rich curriculum: set high expectations for oracy, value every voice through pairs, trios and cold calling, teach oracy explicitly within subject content, harness oracy to elevate learning, and appraise progress lightly. He opposes adding oracy assessment to public exams and argues that the talk is in service of the curriculum, not an extra. His conclusion is that a knowledge-rich, experience-rich curriculum is also oracy-rich, and that deepening learning through talk is the likely next wave of improvement in England.
points: Oracy is not opposed to knowledge: talking about ideas is how students connect new and existing knowledge and strengthen their schema.
Inclusive talk requires structures such as pairs, trios and cold calling so that everyone speaks, plus real listening so cold calls become short dialogues.
Talk structures should be taught explicitly inside geography, science or history lessons rather than as abstract, content-free exercises.
Talk activities should be chosen to elevate the learning, for example elaborative interrogation, paired quizzing or rehearsal for writing, not talk for its own sake.
Appraising oracy can be light and formative, asking students to add, build or challenge, and the author is firmly against assessing oracy in public exams.
quotes: I think there are quite a few false binaries going on which is unhelpful. The main one I want to explore here is that, somehow, oracy is pitted against knowledge.

Oracy to me is predominantly about learning through talk, largely exploratory talk – and, because there are many structures and aspects to talk that help everyone to engage, learning to talk is also embedded in that

We don’t get knowledge and then speak; there’s no neat linear sequence. As we talk about ideas, we engage with them, we connect new and existing knowledge, stretch our schema around and in so doing, we strengthen our understanding.

I see it all the time – students barely given time to grapple with ideas that are half formed, barely given a chance to explore their own understanding and not guided down a path where, by listening to others and exchanging ideas about the topic in hand, they would be able to strengthen their understanding.
Inclusion means that everyone is learning. That means that, with talk, everyone needs to be talking.

You teach the pair-talk routines and expectations as you harness that talk structure to talk about hazards or sustainability or Othello. You teach how to probe deeply into the material intertwined with the material itself – just as you do when teaching how to write about different content.
You don’t just do talk for talk’s sake. You design appropriate talk activities that are most likely to elevate learning in the context of what you’re teaching.
It’s not extra, tick-boxed or an opportunity cost. It’s just a core feature of the whole learning process.
